name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Tuesday 23 June 1981

clue.text: Apt to appease, in the main

blocks.note: first meaning: peace-making, inclined to calm things down
second meaning: the main is the open sea, and this is the name of the largest ocean

explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is an old word for the ocean, so 'in the main' reads like 'mostly' but points to a named sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means peaceable or conciliatory, and it is also the name of the great ocean.

clue.text: Rugby forwards bore military punishment

blocks.note: the forwards in a rugby team form the pack
to bore is to drill a hole

explanation.surface: Rugby forwards were tedious at their army punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like the past of bear or a dull person; it is the verb to make a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: Pack drill was a soldier's punishment of marching in full kit.

clue.text: Fall for 9 of foreign type

blocks.note: the answer to 9 across
de is French for of

explanation.surface: An autumn suited to a foreign sort of person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall' could be autumn; it is a waterfall.
explanation.definitionFit: A cascade is a small waterfall, a fall of water.

clue.text: Musical bean?

definitions.note: an adjective hinting at the instrument, a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: a small whistle-like woodwind pipe
second meaning: a pale green kidney bean, a kind of haricot

explanation.walkthrough: The same French-derived word names a small fipple flute and a kind of haricot bean.
explanation.definitionFit: The flageolet is both a pale green dried bean and a small woodwind pipe.

clue.text: Male crew

blocks.note: surface reading: an all-male team, as of a boat
setter's reading: crew is the old past tense of crow, and the male bird did the crowing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Crew' looks like a noun for a team but is the past tense of crow: 'the cock crew' at Peter's denial.
explanation.definitionFit: The male fowl is the bird that crowed at dawn, as in the Gospels.

clue.text: Two making such a company, like Gilbert's Utopia?

definitions.text: Two making such a company, like Gilbert's Utopia?

blocks.note: surface reading: two's company, the old saying about pairs
setter's reading: a kind of registered firm that once needed only two members, and the second half of the title of a Gilbert and Sullivan opera

explanation.surface: A musing on how two people make a company, as in a Gilbert and Sullivan opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert and Sullivan's opera is 'Utopia, Limited', a satire on joint-stock companies; a private limited company could be formed by just two shareholders.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm whose members' liability is capped is called a limited company, the very word in the opera title.

clue.text: Writings of sovereign are utter nonsense

indicators.note: nonsense is talk without order or sense, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: a sovereign is a one-pound coin: L for pound and I for one
these two words supply the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A dismissal of the monarch's writings as complete rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: A sovereign was a gold coin worth one pound, so it is read as L (the pound sign) and I (one).
explanation.definitionFit: Literature is the body of written works, writings in general.

clue.text: Complaint is a parental afterthought?

blocks.note: a mum is a parent
PS, postscript, is an afterthought added to a letter

explanation.surface: A grievance raised as a parent's last-minute addition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' is an illness, not a grievance; mum is the British word for mom.
explanation.definitionFit: Complaint is a common word for an ailment, and mumps is a childhood illness.

clue.text: Great blow having rent trouble

blocks.note: rent is the past participle of rend, to tear
ado is fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: A huge setback for a tenant in difficulty over the rent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like money paid to a landlord; it means torn.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado is a violent windstorm, a great blow of wind.

clue.text: Worst type of bad form, perhaps

definitions.text: Worst type of bad form, perhaps

blocks.note: surface reading: poor manners or behaviour
setter's reading: a form is a school class, and the worst pupil in a weak class

explanation.walkthrough: In British schools a 'form' is a class or year group, so 'bad form' is a poor class, not bad manners.
explanation.definitionFit: A dunce is the slowest pupil in the class, traditionally made to wear a pointed cap.

clue.text: Envious Roman returns bills to another

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way one came, so the letters are read from the far end

blocks.note: AC is the abbreviation for account, a bill; plural ACS
one more account, AC again

explanation.surface: A jealous Roman sends his unpaid bills back to somebody else.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Antony in Julius Caesar speaks of 'the envious Casca' as he shows the rents in Caesar's cloak.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Antony calls this conspirator envious, so the phrase identifies one particular Roman.

clue.text: Many a river has an additional boat

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, i.e. many
taken as written
the Tamar divides Devon from Cornwall, and also flows through Tasmania
an extra AN is tacked on at the end

explanation.surface: Many rivers have a second boat moored on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Many' as C is a crossword staple from the Roman numeral for 100.
explanation.definitionFit: A twin-hulled sailing vessel is a kind of boat.

clue.text: Bill's party clothes in it?

definitions.note: a description of the thing rather than a synonym

blocks.note: first meaning: the party who writes out a bill of exchange or cheque
second meaning: a sliding box in a chest where clothes are kept

explanation.surface: Someone called Bill is throwing a party and wondering what to wear to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name, but it is a bill of exchange; 'party' is the legal sense, a person in a transaction.
explanation.definitionFit: In banking, the person who issues a bill or cheque is its drawer, and a chest of drawers stores clothing.

clue.text: A sort of riding habit — period

blocks.note: a habit is a garment, as in a riding habit
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A historical note on a style of riding habit worn in a certain era.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riding habit' reads as one phrase for the outfit, but the definition stops at 'riding' and 'habit' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the equestrian discipline of training a horse to perform precise movements, a form of riding.

clue.text: Members of IRA meet VIP in this mood

indicators.note: the words that follow are treated as a pool of member letters, to be gathered in any order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Republican paramilitaries meet a dignitary, and the atmosphere is tense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mood' is the grammar term: the verb form used for commands.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar the imperative is the mood of commands, like 'go' or 'sit'.

clue.text: Ladies almost wild to achieve perfection

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the word is dropped
wild suggests something out of control, so the letters run loose into a new order

blocks.note: the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: Women going nearly wild in pursuit of the perfect result.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun this names a standard of perfection one aims for.

clue.text: It gives time to take the strain

definitions.text: It gives time to take the strain

blocks.clueFragment: It gives time to take the strain
blocks.note: surface reading: something that allows a breather from stress or pressure
setter's reading: a strain is a piece of music, and the device keeps the beat for a musician playing it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Time' is musical tempo and 'strain' is a melody, not stress; the clicking device beats time for whoever plays.
explanation.definitionFit: A ticking device sets the tempo for a musician, giving time to a tune.

clue.text: Chips, perhaps, from the painting

blocks.note: first meaning: Mr Chips, the elderly schoolmaster of 'Goodbye, Mr Chips', is an example of a veteran teacher
second meaning: a picture by a great European artist before about 1800

explanation.surface: Bits flaking off a painting, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chips' reads as fragments of paint (or fried potatoes); capitalised it is the schoolmaster in James Hilton's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Chips is a schoolmaster grown old, and a canvas by an early great artist is likewise called by this name.

clue.text: Formerly coming out of pressing necessity

blocks.note: first meaning: in older English the word meant the act of rising up or appearing
second meaning: an urgent crisis needing immediate action

explanation.surface: Something that once emerged from an urgent need.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Formerly' flags an archaic sense: the word once meant emergence.
explanation.definitionFit: Today the word names a sudden crisis demanding action; its obsolete sense was simply emerging.

clue.text: Short time — long distance

blocks.note: surface reading: the first half sounds like a brief span of time, an easy year
setter's reading: astronomers use the term as a vast measure of length

explanation.walkthrough: The name pairs 'light', which can mean easy or slight, with 'year', yet it measures length, not time: how far light travels in a year.
explanation.definitionFit: Astronomers use this unit for enormous distances, about nine and a half trillion kilometres.

clue.text: PG has Arlen novel — boarders want it

indicators.note: novel means new or fresh, so the letters take a new form

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A publisher's note that a lodger wants a copy of the latest Michael Arlen novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boarders' sound like lodgers; they are pirates boarding a ship, who throw a grappling hook.
explanation.definitionFit: A grapnel is a grappling iron, the hooked tool used to seize and board another vessel.

clue.text: Song for keener types

blocks.note: surface reading: people who are more enthusiastic
setter's reading: a keener is a mourner who keens, wailing for the dead, and this is their lament

explanation.walkthrough: 'Keener' looks like the comparative of keen; here it is a noun, one who keens, as at an Irish wake.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow mournful song of lament for the dead suits professional mourners.

clue.text: Robin gets fish all right — about 100

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: a rudd is a freshwater fish
OK means all right
C is the Roman numeral for 100

explanation.surface: A robin catches a fish and is fine, roughly a hundred times.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruddock is an old country name for the robin, from its ruddy breast.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruddock is a dialect or archaic name for the European robin.

clue.text: Guide gets in an empty Pullman

indicators.note: to get in is to enter, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: read as pull-man: DRAG is pull, plus MAN
something empty holds nothing, a zero, O

explanation.surface: A tour guide boards an empty Pullman railway carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: A Pullman is a luxury rail carriage; split it as 'pull man'. The scan's 'us' must be 'in', since nothing else explains putting O inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A dragoman was an interpreter and guide in Arabic, Turkish or Persian-speaking lands.

clue.text: Birds in trousers?

blocks.note: first meaning: waterfowl with flat bills
second meaning: white trousers made of a heavy cotton cloth

explanation.surface: A puzzled picture of birds wearing trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: Ducks are trousers of duck, a strong cotton or linen fabric, often worn by sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: The waterbird name doubles as the fabric, and garments made from that cloth.

clue.text: Hunter turned up in a peignoir — odd!

indicators.note: in says the word sits inside the run of letters that follows
in a down clue, turned up means read from the bottom upwards, against the usual direction

blocks.note: the letters spanning the end of one word and start of the next

explanation.surface: A hunter strangely turns up wearing a lady's dressing gown.
explanation.walkthrough: A peignoir is a woman's light dressing gown.
explanation.definitionFit: Orion is the great hunter of Greek myth, set among the stars as a constellation.

clue.text: Ferocious animal makes players go back

indicators.note: back means in the opposite direction, so the letters of the verb are written from right to left

blocks.note: a band is a group of musicians, players
taken as written, then turned round

explanation.surface: A savage beast forces the team to retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players' suggests a sports team, but they are musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandog is a fierce mastiff kept chained, an aggressive guard animal.

clue.text: Speed of a flier

blocks.note: first meaning: a nautical mile per hour, the unit of speed at sea
second meaning: a small wading sandpiper

explanation.surface: How fast an aviator goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests a pilot; it is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The knot measures ships' and aircraft speed, and is also a shorebird of the sandpiper family.

clue.text: Well, what a state you're in!

definitions.text: Well, what a state you're in!

blocks.note: surface reading: an exclamation at somebody's dishevelled or agitated appearance
setter's reading: being well means being in good shape, and 'state you're in' describes the general word for fitness or shape

explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' reads as an exclamation opening the sentence, but it is also the adjective for healthy: in good form.
explanation.definitionFit: This word names the state something or someone is in, including fitness or health.

clue.text: A god given name of an ancient character

blocks.note: Thor is the Norse god of thunder
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A deity is handed the name of a figure from antiquity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' looks like a person in a story; it is a letter of an alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Thorn is the old runic letter þ used in Old English for the th sound.

clue.text: Shakespeare's justice demanding it in court?

definitions.note: a description: the thing an usher calls for

blocks.note: first meaning: the country justice paired with Shallow in Henry IV Part 2
second meaning: what a court usher calls for when the judge enters

explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 2 has two rustic justices, Shallow and his cousin, whose name is also the cry for quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: The minor justice's surname is the word an usher shouts to hush a courtroom.

clue.text: Act, taking note from prison officer

blocks.note: a turn is a stage act or performance
a key is a musical scale, a tonal note-system; it is added on

explanation.surface: A performance that borrows a memo from a jail guard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act' looks like a verb; it is a music-hall turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A turnkey is an old word for a jailer, the one holding the keys.
